cards.front: Why does AR need computer vision at all?
cards.back: Inertial sensors give orientation but **never position** — a bias double-integrates into quadratic error. Outside a prepared room the only sensor supplying an **absolute spatial reference** is the **camera**. Vision closes the loop inertial sensing cannot.

cards.front: The six tracking methods
cards.back: **Marker based** (predefined visual markers) · **Infrared** (retro-reflective spheres + IR cameras) · **Natural feature** (Harris, FAST, SIFT, SURF) · **SLAM** (model-free real-time mapping and localisation) · **Visual odometry** (essential matrix, 5-point in RANSAC) · **PTAM** (tracking and mapping in separate threads).

cards.front: Sparse vs dense tracking
cards.back: **Sparse** — **discrete interest points**, ordinary cameras, cheap; gives camera pose. **Dense** — **every pixel**, needs **rich sensory input** (depth sensor like Kinect); gives pose **and a surface model**, enabling **continuous body-part tracking** and **occlusion handling**.

cards.front: The two axes that organise all tracking methods
cards.back: **Prepared vs unprepared environment** — markers/IR need setup and buy accuracy; natural feature/SLAM need nothing and buy deployability. **Sparse vs dense** — points vs every pixel. Together they place every method.

cards.front: The four tracking layers by timescale
cards.back: **Inertial** (1000 Hz, what changed this millisecond) → **frame-to-frame** (incremental tracking, VO) → **mapping** (SLAM, keyframes) → **relocalisation** (tracking by detection, bag-of-words). Systems **fall back down the stack** when a layer fails.

cards.front: The five stages of marker tracking
cards.back: **① Capture** → **② thresholding/binarization** → **③ detect quadrilateral contours & identify the pattern** → **④ pose estimation** (homography → 6DOF) → **⑤ render**. **ARToolKit** is the named example.

cards.front: Why do four corners give full 6DOF from one image?
cards.back: The marker is a **square of known size**, so the 3D corner coordinates are known. Four **3D↔2D correspondences** is a small **PnP** problem. **Known geometry converts a single image into an absolute pose** — no history, no map, no motion.

cards.front: What does a marker give that monocular natural-feature tracking cannot?
cards.back: **Absolute scale.** A single camera cannot distinguish a doll's house from a real one — identical images. The marker's known physical size dissolves the ambiguity, which is why markers are still used to **bootstrap SLAM maps with correct scale**.

cards.front: The five-stage IR motion capture pipeline
cards.back: **① Blob detection** in all images → **② point correspondence via epipolar geometry** → **③ triangulation** to 3D candidates → **④ match to known 3D target points** → **⑤ pose via absolute orientation**.

cards.front: What does epipolar geometry solve in the IR pipeline?
cards.back: **Correspondence** — which blob in camera A is which blob in camera B. The constraint $\mathbf x_B^{\mathsf T} F \mathbf x_A = 0$ means the match must lie on a **single line**, turning a 2D search into a **1D** one. Not detection, not pose.

cards.front: Why retro-reflective spheres and IR ring lights?
cards.back: Retro-reflective material returns light **straight back to its source**, so with IR LEDs ringing each camera the spheres blaze and everything else is dark. **Engineer the image to be trivial** rather than making the algorithm robust — hence sub-millimetre accuracy at 200–400 Hz.

cards.front: Absolute orientation — what kind of problem?
cards.back: **3D↔3D alignment** with a **closed-form solution** (Horn / SVD): $\min_{R,\mathbf t}\sum\lVert(R\mathbf p_i + \mathbf t) - \mathbf q_i\rVert^2$. Easier than marker tracking's **3D↔2D** PnP — that simplification is what multiple cameras buy you.

cards.front: Why corners rather than edges or flat regions?
cards.back: **Flat** — shifting the window changes nothing: no information. **Edge** — no change along its length: one dimension (the **aperture problem**). **Corner** — changes in **every** direction: two dimensions, fully localisable.

cards.front: Harris corner detector
cards.back: Uses the **structure tensor** of local gradients; its two **eigenvalues** classify the region — both small = flat, one large = edge, **both large = corner**. Response $R = \det(M) - k(\text{tr}M)^2$ avoids computing eigenvalues. **Rotation-invariant but not scale-invariant**.

cards.front: FAST, and why it is fast
cards.back: A pixel is a corner if a **contiguous arc of ≥9** of the 16 pixels on a surrounding circle are all brighter or all darker. Speed comes from testing **only pixels 1, 5, 9 and 13 first** — at least three must agree, so most candidates are rejected after **four comparisons**.

cards.front: SIFT and SURF — what they add
cards.back: **Scale invariance.** SIFT finds extrema in a **Difference-of-Gaussians scale space**, giving each keypoint a **characteristic scale** and **orientation**; descriptor is **128-D**. SURF approximates it with **box filters + integral images** — several times faster, **64-D**. **ORB** (FAST + binary descriptor) is the mobile-era replacement.

cards.front: Detector vs descriptor
cards.back: **Detector** answers *'where are the interesting points?'* → a location (+ scale, orientation). **Descriptor** answers *'what does this point look like?'* → a **vector** enabling matching. **Detector finds; descriptor recognises.**

cards.front: The five stages of tracking by detection
cards.back: **① Interest point detection → ② descriptor creation → ③ descriptor matching → ④ Perspective-n-Point camera pose determination → ⑤ robust pose estimation (RANSAC).** You need **correspondences before pose** — that's why matching precedes PnP.

cards.front: What does PnP solve?
cards.back: Given $n$ **3D↔2D** correspondences (known 3D points and their image projections), recover the camera's **6DOF pose**. **P3P** gives up to four solutions from three points; a fourth disambiguates. It is the same problem marker tracking solves with four square corners.

cards.front: Why RANSAC, and how does it work?
cards.back: Descriptor matching **always produces outliers** and least squares isn't robust to them. RANSAC: **sample minimally → fit → count inliers → keep the best → refit on inliers**. It **inverts the usual logic** — guess a clean sample and ask how many agree; consensus identifies the good data.

cards.front: Tracking by detection vs incremental — the trade
cards.back: **By detection**: stateless, **no drift**, **instant recovery**, handles fast motion — but **expensive every frame** and needs a **pre-built map**. **Incremental**: cheap and smooth — but **drifts** and **cannot self-recover**. Real systems run **incremental for speed, detection for recovery**.

cards.front: What technique does KLT use?
cards.back: **Feature extraction followed by optical flow tracking.** It minimises $\sum[I_{t+1}(\mathbf x + \mathbf d) - I_t(\mathbf x)]^2$ over a small window, using the optical-flow constraint $I_xu + I_yv + I_t = 0$ — solvable exactly where the structure tensor has **two large eigenvalues**, i.e. at corners.

cards.front: Patch warping and the five failure conditions
cards.back: Models how a patch **rotates, scales and shears** with viewpoint (affine or homography warp), not just where it moved. The course's failure cases: **losing target, occlusion, tilt, motion blur, reflection** — each breaks the **brightness constancy** assumption optical flow depends on.

cards.front: Camera motion models for active search
cards.back: **Constant position** (static shots) · **constant velocity** (the common default) · **constant acceleration** (aggressive motion) · **IMU-driven** (best when available — actual motion at 1000 Hz). A tighter prediction means a **smaller search window**: faster and less likely to latch onto the wrong feature.

cards.front: Incremental tracking — advantages and drawbacks
cards.back: **Pros:** computationally cheap, high frame rates, **smooth/low-jitter** pose, no map needed. **Cons:** **drift accumulates without bound**; fails on fast motion, occlusion, blur and lighting change; **cannot recover** once lost; needs initialisation.

cards.front: What is SLAM, and what is the chicken-and-egg problem?
cards.back: **Model-free, real-time mapping and localization without prior models.** To know where you are you need a **map**; to build a map you need to know **where you are**. Resolved by **bootstrapping** — and the interesting parts are all about stopping the errors compounding.

cards.front: The four SLAM components
cards.back: **Front end (tracking)** — pose against the existing map. **Back end (mapping)** — add and refine landmarks, **bundle adjustment**. **Loop closure** — recognise a visited place and **correct drift**. **Relocalisation** — recover after failure via tracking by detection.

cards.front: Why is loop closure so important?
cards.back: It is the **visual equivalent of an absolute reference**. Incremental tracking drifts exactly as a gyroscope does; recognising a previously-mapped place is a measurement **independent of history**, so it cancels accumulated error — producing SLAM's characteristic map **snap**.

cards.front: PTAM's two threads
cards.back: **Tracking thread — full frame rate, computing camera poses from correspondences.** **Mapping thread — much slower, adding new keyframes** and running bundle adjustment. Remember by purpose: **tracking feeds the display so it must never be late; mapping improves the map so it can afford to think.**

cards.front: Why keyframes?
cards.back: Most frames are nearly identical to their neighbours and add nothing. Keyframes are selected on **time/distance, view change (baseline) and tracking quality**, and bundle adjustment runs over **keyframes only** — turning an unbounded stream into a bounded graph.

cards.front: SLAM's limitations
cards.back: **Textureless environments** · **dynamic scenes** (moving people violate the static-world assumption) · **repetitive structure** causing **false loop closures** · computational cost and battery · drift between closures · **scale ambiguity** for a single camera without inertial or stereo input.

cards.front: The visual odometry pipeline
cards.back: **Capture & undistort → detect and track features → estimate the essential matrix (5-point in RANSAC) → decompose into $R$ and $\mathbf t$ → resolve the four-fold ambiguity (cheirality) → recover scale externally → concatenate onto the trajectory.**

cards.front: Why does the essential matrix have 5 DOF?
cards.back: 3 rotation + 3 translation **− 1**, because **translation magnitude is unrecoverable** from images. Hence the **5-point algorithm** — and fewer points per RANSAC sample means dramatically fewer iterations than the old 8-point method.

cards.front: Essential vs fundamental matrix
cards.back: **$F$** relates points in raw **pixel** coordinates and needs no calibration. **$E$** relates points in **normalised camera** coordinates and requires the **intrinsics $K$** ($E = K'^{\mathsf T}FK$). Because $E$ encodes calibrated geometry, it **decomposes into $R$ and $\mathbf t$** — $F$ cannot.

cards.front: How is scale recovered in visual odometry?
cards.back: It can't be, from a single camera alone. External cues: **stereo baseline** · **IMU** (measures m/s², giving metric scale) · a **known object or marker** · a **depth sensor** · an **assumed camera height** (automotive). **Scale drift** is the related nuisance, corrected by loop closure.

cards.front: Visual odometry vs SLAM
cards.back: **VO is SLAM's front end without the memory** — trajectory only, recent frames only, **no loop closure**, so drift is **unbounded**. SLAM adds a persistent map and loop closure, converting unbounded drift into **bounded** error. VO ≈ dead reckoning; SLAM ≈ dead reckoning plus recognised landmarks.

cards.front: The three outdoor tracking techniques
cards.back: **Sensor fusion** — GPS + IMU + visual · **GIS data integration** — building outlines and elevation models · **scalable visual matching** — **bag-of-words** place recognition.

cards.front: GPS vs vision outdoors — the division of labour
cards.back: **GPS says which building you are near; vision says exactly where on it to draw.** GPS is 1–100 m — far too coarse for registration, but it **bounds the search globally**. Vision refines to centimetres locally but has no idea which city it's in.

cards.front: How does bag-of-words scale place recognition?
cards.back: **Throw away the geometry, then put it back.** Cluster descriptors into ~$10^6$ **visual words**; represent each image as a **word histogram**; search via an **inverted index** with **TF-IDF** weighting; then **geometric verification (RANSAC)** on the shortlist. Cheap-and-approximate shortlists; expensive-and-exact confirms.

cards.front: What does GIS data contribute?
cards.back: **Building footprints** (predict visible façades), **elevation models** (terrain and occlusion), **3D city models** (register the skyline), **road networks/POIs** (semantic anchors). **Constraints are information** — a prior that turns open-ended pose search into model fitting, and enables **occlusion**.

cards.front: Why does AR need 3D scanning as well as tracking?
cards.back: Tracking gives **camera pose**; scanning gives **scene geometry** — required for **occlusion** (depth per pixel), **physics** (collision mesh), **placement** (plane detection), **realistic lighting** and **persistence**. Without it content **floats** rather than inhabiting the room.

cards.front: Active 3D scanning methods
cards.back: **Structured light** — project a known pattern, measure deformation (**Kinect v1**); indoor only. **Time-of-Flight** — measure return time per pixel, $d = c\Delta t/2$ (Kinect v2); multipath errors. **LIDAR** — swept laser (iPhone Pro); **long range, works outdoors**.

cards.front: Passive 3D scanning methods
cards.back: **Stereo** — two cameras, known **baseline**, depth from **disparity**; cheap and works outdoors but **fails on textureless surfaces**. **Photogrammetry / SfM** — many overlapping photos, bundle adjustment for poses **and** structure; very high fidelity but **offline** and **no absolute scale** without a reference.

cards.front: The reconstruction pipeline
cards.back: **① Capture → ② register** (ICP for depth scans, feature matching for images) **→ ③ fuse** into a **TSDF** volume **→ ④ mesh** (marching cubes) **→ ⑤ texture.** Fusing into a volume **averages away noise** and defines a true surface — a raw point cloud has no inside/outside.

cards.front: Active vs passive — the choosing rule
cards.back: **Active methods supply their own light**, so they work on blank walls and in the dark but are washed out by sunlight. **Passive methods rely on existing texture**, so they fail on plain surfaces but work in daylight. Two questions: **is there texture?** and **is there sunlight?**

cards.front: The five interaction design considerations
cards.back: **Ergonomics** (avoid **gorilla arm**) · **input multimodality** (gestures, voice, gaze, touch) · **output diversity** (visual, auditory, haptic) · **occlusion and physical–virtual coherence** · **latency reduction**.

cards.front: Gorilla arm — definition and mitigations
cards.back: Fatigue from holding the arm **unsupported in mid-air**; the deltoid isn't built for sustained static load. Mitigations: keep interaction **below shoulder height**, prefer **short gestures over sustained poses**, allow the arm to **rest** (palm/hand-referenced UI, controllers held low), use **gaze or voice** for frequent actions.

cards.front: The three AR placement frames
cards.back: **Head-referenced** — fixed to gaze; always available but **always occluding**. **Torso-referenced** — virtual **toolbelts**; out of the way, needs a deliberate turn. **Hand/arm-referenced** — **palm displays**, gesture UIs; costs a hand. (Plus **world-referenced**, which needs full 6DOF registration.)

cards.front: The seven input modalities
cards.back: **Gestures** (pinch, swipe, frame, wave — depth sensors) · **touch** (LucidTouch, back-of-device) · **voice** (NLP) · **gaze** · **rigid body manipulation** (VR controllers) · **body tracking** (Kinect, Leap Motion) · **multimodal**.

cards.front: The two recurring interaction failures
cards.back: **Gorilla arm** — mid-air fatigue. **The Midas touch problem** — the system can't distinguish intentional from incidental input, so it triggers when you didn't mean it. Gaze suffers it worst (you can't look without selecting); **pinch** is popular because hands rarely pinch by accident.

cards.front: Why is gaze the fastest pointing modality, and why is it never used alone?
cards.back: **Fastest** because the eye reaches a target before the hand starts moving, and it's effortless — you were going to look anyway. **Never alone** because of the Midas touch problem; the fix is **gaze-and-commit** (gaze to point, pinch/dwell/voice to confirm).

cards.front: Why do controllers survive hand tracking?
cards.back: They provide **buttons** (unambiguous, no Midas touch), **haptic feedback** (felt confirmation), a **physical object to grip** (proprioception locates your hand without looking), and **support** — a hand holding a controller rests lower, reducing **gorilla arm**.

cards.front: Multimodal interaction — the principle
cards.back: **Use each modality for what it is good at**: speech for **verbs and names**, gaze/gesture for **deixis** (*this, that, there*). The canonical demo is **'Put that there'** (Bolt, 1980). It also adds **robustness** — sensor fusion applied to intent rather than pose.

cards.front: The six output modalities
cards.back: **Head-referenced displays** · **torso/hand/arm-referenced UI overlays** · **magic lenses** (augmented browsing — navigation, tourism) · **projector-based AR** · **spatial audio** (3D sound cues) · **haptics** (force feedback, e.g. **Phantom Omni**).

cards.front: What is a magic lens?
cards.back: A **movable window revealing a different view of whatever is behind it** — augment only what's **inside the lens**, solving the clutter problem. **Every phone AR app is a magic lens**: you move the window, not the world.

cards.front: Tactile vs kinaesthetic haptics
cards.back: **Tactile (cutaneous)** — stimulates **skin**; conveys **texture, vibration, contact** (controller rumble, ultrasonic mid-air). **Kinaesthetic (force)** — stimulates **muscles and joints**; conveys **weight, resistance, stiffness** (**Phantom Omni**, exoskeleton gloves).

cards.front: Why must haptics update at ~1000 Hz?
cards.back: Touch is **far more temporally acute than vision** — a millisecond discontinuity is felt as a buzz, whereas vision integrates over tens of milliseconds. **A surface updating at 60 Hz feels like jelly, not a wall.** It's the haptic counterpart of the visual 20 ms budget.

cards.front: Why is spatial audio disproportionately valuable in AR/VR?
cards.back: **Hearing is omnidirectional; vision is not.** A visual cue outside the (narrow) headset FOV is invisible, but a **sound behind you** is heard instantly and tells you where to look — making audio the natural channel for **notification and guidance**.

cards.front: Sound as a physical phenomenon
cards.back: A **longitudinal pressure wave** — molecules oscillate **along** the direction of travel, creating compressions and rarefactions. It **requires a medium** (unlike light). Perception arises from **displacement of the eardrum**, expressed as sound pressure level in **decibels**.

cards.front: Speed of sound and the three frequency ranges
cards.back: **343.2 m/s at 20 °C** (≈ $331 + 0.6T$). **Infrasound < 20 Hz** · **audible 20 Hz – 20 kHz** · **ultrasound > 20 kHz**. The speed explains why **ultrasonic tracking is slow** (~9 ms for 3 m) and why **ITD** works (~640 µs max).

cards.front: The four wave behaviours and their AR/VR effects
cards.back: **Reflection** → echoes and **reverberation** (room size, material) · **transmission** → muffled sound through walls · **refraction** → bending through gradients (minor indoors) · **diffraction** → **hearing around corners**.

cards.front: Why is audio occlusion a filter, not a block?
cards.back: **Diffraction is frequency-dependent.** Audible wavelengths (**1.7 cm to 17 m**) are comparable to doors and furniture, so **low frequencies bend around obstacles while high frequencies are blocked**. Light (~500 nm) never diffracts at human scale — hence graphics occlusion is binary and audio occlusion is a **low-pass filter**.

cards.front: Monaural localisation cues
cards.back: **Pinna effects** — the outer ear's folds filter direction-dependently, resolving **up/down and front/back** where binaural cues fail. **Amplitude** — louder means nearer. **Spectrum attenuation** — air absorbs highs, so distant sounds are duller. Personalisation matters: a generic **HRTF** belongs to someone else's ears.

cards.front: ITD and ILD — and why they split by frequency
cards.back: **ITD** (nearer ear first) works at **low frequencies**: above ~1.5 kHz the wavelength is shorter than the ear spacing so **phase wraps ambiguously**. **ILD** (head shadow) works at **high frequencies**: the head only casts a shadow when the wavelength is **smaller than the head** — long waves **diffract around it**. This is **duplex theory**.

cards.front: The cone of confusion
cards.back: A **hyperboloid of positions giving identical ITD and ILD** — front and back are indistinguishable from binaural cues alone. Resolved by **head movements** (cues change differently for front vs back) and **pinna filtering**. A strong argument for **head-tracked spatial audio**.

cards.front: The four psychoacoustic principles
cards.back: **Stevens' power law** — $\psi = k\phi^{0.67}$; loudness is non-linear, so ~10× power to double perceived loudness (hence dB and **logarithmic volume controls**). **JND** — smallest perceivable change, a constant **ratio** (Weber). **Pitch discrimination** — resolution worsens as frequency rises. **Precedence effect** — the **first wavefront** determines direction.

cards.front: Why the precedence effect matters for VR audio
cards.back: It's why you can localise a source in a reverberant room at all — the brain trusts **only the first arrival**, since only that took the direct path. So VR audio can be economical: **the direct path must be accurate and low-latency, while reflections can be approximated** — they give spaciousness, not direction.

cards.front: The three reactive AI techniques
cards.back: **FSM** — rule-based state transitions; simple and predictable but transitions grow $O(n^2)$. **Behaviour trees** — hierarchical; sequence (AND), selector (OR), decorator, leaf; **modular and reusable**. **Utility AI** — score every action $U(a)=\sum w_if_i$; **most adaptable**, hardest to predict.

cards.front: Why behaviour trees replaced FSMs
cards.back: Priority is **implicit in the structure**, so adding a behaviour means inserting **one subtree** rather than re-wiring $n$ transitions. Subtrees are **reusable**, and root-down re-evaluation gives **automatic interruption** when a higher-priority condition becomes true. **Modularity is the win.**

cards.front: Reactive AI on the four syllabus properties
cards.back: **Adaptability** — limited; bounded by what was authored. **Complexity** — grows badly ($O(n^2)$ FSM transitions). **Universality** — low; written for one character in one game, doesn't transfer. **Feasibility** — **excellent**: trivial cost, predictable, debuggable, designer-authorable. It trades adaptability for feasibility, and in real-time systems that's usually right.

cards.front: Reactive vs deliberative in one line
cards.back: **Reactive asks *'what do I do now?'*; deliberative asks *'what sequence will get me what I want?'*.** A deliberative agent **searches over possible futures** and produces a **plan** — behaviour nobody authored, which fell out of the search.

cards.front: The three problems deliberative AI solves
cards.back: **Resource management** · **tactical planning** · **intelligent exploration**. All share one feature: **the best action now depends on what happens later** — exactly what a reactive rule (a function of the present only) cannot express.

cards.front: Deliberative AI's two trade-offs
cards.back: **Less controllable than reactive AI** — a planner may find a technically optimal solution that ruins a designed set-piece. **Computationally intensive**, though it **can be offloaded offline** — plan ahead and cache, plan on a background thread, or plan coarsely above a reactive layer.

cards.front: The four comparison axes (exam question)
cards.back: **Adaptability** — deliberative wins (composes novel plans). **Predictability** — reactive wins (same input, same output). **Control** — reactive wins (designer authors behaviour directly). **Efficiency** — reactive wins (trivial cost vs search). Hence the **hybrid architecture**.

cards.front: The hybrid AI architecture
cards.back: **Deliberative on top** (slow, occasional, sets goals: *'get the key, then the door, then escape'*) over **reactive underneath** (every tick, fast: *'walk there, dodge, open'*). **Fast-and-dumb under slow-and-smart** — the same pattern as IMU under vision, and PTAM's tracking thread under its mapping thread.

cards.front: The four learning paradigms in AR/VR
cards.back: **Supervised** — inputs to labelled outputs (image → pose). **Unsupervised** — structure discovery (clustering). **Reinforcement** — trial and error via **rewards**. **Imitation** — from **human demonstration**.

cards.front: What makes reinforcement learning hard?
cards.back: Feedback is **delayed and evaluative, not instructive**. Supervised learning is told *'the answer was X'*; RL is told only *'those fifty actions eventually scored 7'* and must work out which deserved credit — the **credit assignment problem**. Hence the need for enormous numbers of trials.

cards.front: The three imitation learning approaches
cards.back: **Behaviour cloning** — supervised on (state, action) pairs; cheap but suffers **compounding error**. **Inverse RL** — infers the **reward function** the expert was optimising; robust but very expensive. **GAIL** — a **discriminator** distinguishes expert from agent trajectories and acts as the reward; IRL-quality at closer to cloning cost.

cards.front: Behaviour cloning's compounding error
cards.back: Trained only on states the **expert visited**. One small mistake puts the agent in a state the expert never occupied, so the next action is worse and the error snowballs. A policy cloned from perfect driving has **never seen the car drifting toward the kerb** — so it never learned to recover.

cards.front: The five ML applications in AR/VR
cards.back: **Object recognition** — **YOLO, SSD** (single-pass, fast enough for a frame budget) · **gesture recognition** — **optical flow, KLT** · **SLAM with neural networks** · **procedural content generation** — **GANs** · **adaptive NPCs** — **RL agents**.
